The dilruba is a bowed instrument from India, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-7, of the bowed-sitar kind, a little larger than the esraj, with a bigger, square soundbox and close to the sarangi. It has a long neck, about twenty movable metal frets, four metal main strings and more than twenty sympathetic strings, and only the leftmost main string is bowed; the soundbox is a hollowed gourd or carved wood covered with goatskin. The player sits with the body in front of the knees or on the lap, the neck against the left shoulder, the right hand holding the bow, and the left hand sliding up and down the strings to make the slides. It is closely tied to Sikh history and can accompany the ragis at the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple).
迪爾魯巴琴演奏者坐姿，將琴底置於身前或腿上，琴頸靠左肩。右手持弓，只拉最左側主弦: The dilruba player sits with the base of the instrument in front of the body or on the lap, the neck against the left shoulder. The right hand holds the bow and bows only the leftmost main string; the left hand stops the strings along about twenty movable metal frets to change the pitch. Beginners steady the hold and the bowing first, then practise sliding the left hand up and down to make the slides, rather than pulling the string sideways across the frets as on the sitar.

迪爾魯巴琴起源印度，有版本可追溯至三、四世紀。傳統起源故事認為，約三百年前由第十: The dilruba comes from India, and some versions go back to the third or fourth century. A traditional origin story holds that about three hundred years ago the tenth Sikh guru, Guru Gobind Singh, adapted it from the older, heavier taus so that the Khalsa army could carry it on horseback; scholars doubt this, and other keepers of the kirtan tradition link it to the patronage of Maharaja Bhupinder Singh and to Mahant Gajja Singh. After the British Indian introduction of the harmonium it declined, because its learning curve was steeper. In the 1960s it spread through the Beatles' song Within You Without You; since 2006 it has accompanied the ragis at the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple), and it is taught more often in India and abroad.
